papers.title_in_file: Exploring the role of parameters in variational quantum algorithms
papers.version_note: arXiv:2209.14405v1, dated September 30, 2022 on the first page; the text matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A preprint that proposes the Lie rank of the dynamical Lie algebra as a design metric for Pauli-based variational circuits and tests it on a 2 x 2 XXZ-Heisenberg model.

existing.note: The abstract sentence holds, but the body limits it: the only application is one 2 x 2 XXZ-Heisenberg system, the Conclusion calls the work preliminary explorations, and the energy experiment compares the VHA with the LAP energy by parameter count and layers, not Lie rank against energy directly. The LAP ansatz, with the full Lie algebra, reached only -1.0721 against a ground state energy of -1.9794.
existing.value: The authors report, from numerical experiments on one XXZ-Heisenberg model, that the Lie rank criterion positively correlates with the ability of the Pauli-based ansatz to approximate ground-state energies, and describe this as preliminary explorations.
existing.anchor: Abstract p.1; Section V Conclusion p.9
quotes: Through numerical experiments, we ﬁnd that the Lie rank criterion of the Hamiltonian that deﬁnes the system ansatz positively correlates with the ability of the Pauli-based ansatz to approximate ground-state energies.
We have detailed preliminary explorations on how the choice of parametrization in variational Hamiltonian ansätze aﬀects the expressive capability of such ansätze using the XXZ-Heisenberg model.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one model.
existing.reader_inference: The text reports no correlation statistic and no direct plot of energy against Lie rank.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing earlier work, that Lloyd used Lie algebraic arguments to show that QAOA is computationally universal, a proof formalized later by Morales and coauthors.
quotes: Lloyd [11] used Lie algebraic arguments to show that QAOA is computationally universal, a proof that was formalized later by Morales et al. [12].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper reports, citing earlier work on MAX-2SAT and MAX-3-SAT problems solved with QAOA, that beyond a critical constraints-to-variables ratio the QAOA ansatz shows reachability deficits: it does not cover enough of the Hilbert space to contain the target state.
quotes: They applied the QAOA approach from Ref. [12] to study MAX-2SAT and MAX-3-SAT optimization problem [16].

The authors found that beyond a critical constraints-tovariables ratio in the problem setting, the algorithm exhibits reachability deﬁcits, that is the QAOA ansatz does not cover a suﬃciently large portion of the Hilbert space to contain the target state.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result, attributed to Ref. [14].

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that hardware-efficient circuits seem random from the problem Hamiltonian standpoint and that their optimization landscape is plagued by barren plateaus, where the average gradient magnitude approaches zero for circuits of even modest parameter scaling with respect to the number of qubits.
quotes: of this method is that the quantum circuits seem random from the problem Hamiltonian standpoint.

Consequently, their optimization landscape is plagued by the barren plateaus problem [22]: the average gradient magnitude approaches zero for circuits of even modest parameter scaling with respect to the number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result (Ref. [22]).

assertions.value: The paper states, citing Theorem 3.2.1 of d'Alessandro, that the set of reachable states of a controlled system is the connected Lie group associated with the dynamical Lie algebra generated by the control terms.
quotes: Theorem 3.2.1 of d’Alessandro [19] which states that
Theorem 1 The set of reachable states for a system k ck(t)Hˆk is the connected Lie group associated with the dynamical Lie algebra L generated by span{ck}∈C¯{iHˆk}.
assertions.certainty_reason: A theorem the paper attributes to d'Alessandro; the paper does not prove it.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lost the sum sign, so the statement is garbled; the conditions are those of the cited textbook theorem.

assertions.value: The authors define the Lie rank criterion as the dimension of the dynamical Lie algebra of the system, which they describe as the dimension of the vector space in which the controlled system is defined.
quotes: The quantity dim(L) is often referred to as the Lie rank criterion and gives the dimension of that vector space.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the term in Section II B.

assertions.value: The authors state that a system is fully controllable when the dimension of L equals n squared (the dimension of u(n)), and also when it equals n squared minus 1 (the dimension of su(n)), where n is the size of the full Hilbert space.
quotes: The system is fully controllable if dim(L) = n2 = dim(u(n)), where n is the size of the full Hilbert space
The system is also said to be fully controllable when dim(L) = n2 − 1 = dim(su(n))
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the controllability condition as its definition in Section II B.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponent in n2 is printed flat in the text layer; the paper's own appendix uses n squared minus 1 equals 3 for one qubit.

assertions.value: The authors state that they study quantum circuits generated by exponentiating a circuit Hamiltonian written as a linear combination of Pauli strings, which they call Pauli-based PQCs.
quotes: In this article, we are interested in quantum circuits that are generated by unitaries resulting from the exponentiation of a circuit Hamiltonian.
The circuit Hamiltonian Hˆc can generally be written as a linear combination of the Pauli strings

assertions.value: The authors state that the layered ansatz does not exactly implement the exponential map of the Lie algebra; this holds only in the limit of an infinite number of layers, where the first-order Trotter-Suzuki approximation is exact.
quotes: denotes that the proposed layered ansatz approach does not exactly implement the exponential map eL.
The latter is true only in the limit of an inﬁnite number of layers, where the ﬁrst-order Trotter-Suzuki approximation is exact.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its method in Section III A.
assertions.reader_inference: Every reachability and Lie rank result is therefore a statement about the large-layer limit, not about any finite depth.

assertions.value: The authors describe their algorithm for the Lie rank criterion as an iterative procedure that builds a basis of the dynamical Lie algebra from all commutators of its elements, adding each new linearly independent operator, and obtain the Lie rank criterion by counting the elements of the final basis.
quotes: It is an iterative procedure, where a basis for the dynamical Lie algebra of the system is generated using all the commutators of elements of L and appending L whenever a new linearly independent operator is found.
dim(L), or the Lie rank criterion, is obtained by simply counting the number of elements in the ﬁnal basis generated by the algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its procedure in Section III A.

assertions.value: The authors state that the reachable set depends on which Hamiltonian terms carry control functions, and that a system with separate controls on the X term and the Z term is fully controllable, while one control on the sum of the X and Z terms is not.
quotes: For example, the Lie algebra of Hˆ1 = a(t)Xˆ + b(t)Zˆ will be of higher dimension than that of Hˆ2 = c(t)(Xˆ + Zˆ).
In fact, Hˆ1 is fully controllable, while Hˆ2 is not.
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked example stated without a derivation in the body.

assertions.value: The authors show in a one-qubit example that the circuit Hamiltonian X alone has a dynamical Lie algebra of dimension 1, below 3, and cannot reach all one-qubit states, while X plus Y gives a Lie algebra of dimension 3 and is fully controllable.
quotes: The dynamical Lie algebra is L = {iXˆ }, which has a dimension of dim L = 1 < n2 − 1 = 3, where n = 2 is
can not reach all possible one-qubit states.
The dynamical Lie algebra is thus L = {iXˆ , iYˆ , iZˆ}, which has a dimension of dim L = 3 = n2 −1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The appendix derives both cases by hand from the commutator of X and Y.

assertions.value: The authors report that for two qubits they computed the dynamical Lie algebra of every choice of m Pauli strings out of 16, with m from 1 to 16, a total of 65,535 instances, and report the final Lie rank criterion in Fig. 1.

ﬁnal Lie rank criterion value in Fig. 1.

assertions.value: The authors report that full Hilbert space coverage is not possible with fewer than five parametrized terms and is guaranteed with 15 and up, and that full controllability then needs a Lie rank of 15 for two qubits.
quotes: We observe that full Hilbert space coverage is not possible with fewer than ﬁve parametrized terms and is guaranteed with 15 and up.
a system is fully controllable when dim(L) = 4n − 1, hence 15 in our case.

assertions.value: The authors report that the scaling of the Lie rank criterion with the number of parameters is at worst linear and at best exponential, depending on the parametrization.
quotes: Next, we note that the scaling of the Lie rank criterion with the number of parameters is at worst linear and at best exponential, depending on the parametrization.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim comes from fitted curves in Fig. 1 over two qubits only; the text gives no fit quality.

assertions.value: The authors simulate the ferromagnetic ground state energy of the 2 × 2 XXZ-Heisenberg model with ∆/J = −20, whose Hamiltonian has 13 different 4-qubit Pauli terms, using the Variational Hamiltonian Ansatz.
quotes: of the 2 × 2 XXZ-Heisenberg model, with ∆/J = −20.
The resulting Hamiltonian is composed of 13 diﬀerent 4-qubit Pauli terms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its test system in Section IV B.
assertions.reader_inference: One four-qubit system is the only application; the text does not name the optimizer, the shot count or any noise model.

assertions.value: The authors state that they choose a number m from 1 to 13, divide the Hamiltonian terms into m independent sets each receiving one parameter, and for each m uniformly sample a partition from all possible m-parameter partitions.
quotes: We do this by choosing a number m ranging from 1 to 13 and dividing the Hamiltonian terms into m independent sets, each set receiving a controllable parameter.
For all m, we then uniformly sample a partition from all the possible m-parameter partitions
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its sampling method in Section IV B 1.
assertions.reader_inference: The text does not state how many partitions are sampled per m.

assertions.value: The authors report that the maximum Lie rank calculated for the VHA on this model is 61, while full Hilbert space coverage would require a Lie rank of 255, so the VHA, even fully parametrized, is far from expressible enough to cover the full Hilbert space.
quotes: We ﬁrst note that full Hilbert space coverage, which would require a Lie rank of 44 − 1 = 255, is not possible in this case since the maximum Lie rank calculated is 61.
This means that the VHA, even when fully parametrized, is far from being expressible enough to cover the full Hilbert space.
assertions.reader_inference: The 44 is four to the fourth power printed flat; 255 is that power minus 1.

assertions.value: The authors report from Fig. 2 (top) that for a single controllable parameter the distribution of Lie ranks is centered around 1, and that as the number of partitions grows the distribution shifts to re-center around 61, the maximum Lie rank of the VHA.
quotes: From Fig. 2 (top), we observe that for a single controllable parameter (partition) the probability distribution of Lie ranks is centered around 1.
nian, this distribution shifts away from 1 to eventually re-center around 61, the maximum Lie rank one can achieve with the VHA.

assertions.value: The authors report from Fig. 2 (bottom) that the maximum Lie rank is systematically obtained with 12 or more parameters, in some instances with as few as 2, and that with only 4 controllable parameters the probability of reaching the largest Lie rank is already greater than 0.8.
quotes: Fig. 2 (bottom) indicates that the maximum Lie rank is systematically obtained when using ≥ 12 parameters or in some instances comprising of as low as 2 parameters.
Also, with only 4 controllable parameters the probability of reaching the largest Lie rank is already greater than 0.8.

assertions.value: The authors state that four parameters give in principle a Hilbert space coverage similar to a 13-parameter ansatz, but that in practice more layers may be needed because the estimates hold exactly only in the large number of layers limit, and that confirming a high Lie rank for a 4-parameter partition may need more iterations of the algorithm than the 13-parameter case, which needs 1.
quotes: This means that in principle, 4 parameters are enough to achieve a similar Hilbert space coverage than that of a 13-parameter ansatz.
However, in practice, one might have to consider more layers of the ansatz in the 4-parameter case as these estimates hold exactly only in the large number of layers limit.

assertions.value: The authors report from the iteration plots that the mean Lie rank of the different parameterizations increases logistically with the iteration, and that with more controllable parameters the point of inflection shifts to a lower iteration.

However, with an increasing number of controllable parameters in the circuit Hamiltonian, the point of inﬂection shifts to a lower value in iterations.

quotes: Based on these observations, we can deﬁne a function L(x) that approximates the probability of reaching the maximum achievable Lie rank, given a particular Lie rank value at some iteration.
where, a is the mean Lie rank value at the given iteration, α and β are some constants that control the shape of the curve.

assertions.value: The authors state that, using the distribution L(x) built from third-order commutators (Fig. 4), one can approximately predict the reachability of a given parameterization without running the full algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors define the Lie Algebra Partition (LAP) ansatz as a circuit Hamiltonian containing all the terms in the Lie algebra of the fully parameterized XXZ Hamiltonian, which has 61 parameters.
quotes: We ﬁrst use an ansatz with a circuit Hamiltonian containing all the terms in the Lie algebra of fully parameterized XXZ-Hamiltonian and calculate the ground state energy.
The ansatz, referred to as the Lie Algebra Partition (LAP) ansatz, contains 61 parameters (or terms), and is constructed

assertions.value: The authors report that the final optimized energy of the LAP ansatz is -1.0721, far from the actual ground state energy of -1.9794 of the Hamiltonian.
quotes: The ﬁnal optimized energy with the LAP ansatz is -1.0721, which is very far away from the actual ground state energy (-1.9794) of the Hamiltonian.
assertions.reader_inference: Since no VHA instance beat the LAP energy, no ansatz tested in this paper reached the ground state of the model.

assertions.value: The authors state that the large gap between the LAP energy and the ground state energy indicates low reachability of the ansatz: even with 61 parameters it lacks access to the state space holding the ground state.
quotes: This is indicative of the low reachability of the ansatz, as even with 61 parameters, the ansatz does not have access to the state space corresponding to the ground state of the system.
assertions.reader_inference: The text offers no check, such as a different optimizer or restarts, that rules out a failed optimization.

assertions.value: The authors state that using the LAP ansatz directly is not scalable because its circuit depth is exponentially long, but that when feasible optimizing it gives a lower bound on the performance of the VHA or of any P-PQC-based ansatz.
quotes: However, using directly the LAP is not scalable as its circuit depth is exponentially long.
optimizing the LAP ansatz is a powerful tool as it gives a lower bound on the performance of the VHA, or any P-PQC-based ansätze more generally.
assertions.reader_inference: The general claim for any P-PQC is argued from one model; the text gives no proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that all VHA instances with at most 5 variational parameters converge very slowly toward the LAP energy, while instances with at least 6 parameters reach the LAP energy within an error of 10 to the power minus 8 with a small number of circuit layers.
quotes: Indeed, all instances of the VHA with ≤ 5 variational parameters show a very slow convergence towards the LAP energy while instances with ≥ 6 parameters reach the LAP energy within 10−8 of error with a small number of circuit layers.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the only direct energy test in the paper; it compares the VHA to the LAP energy by parameter count, and the text does not plot energy against Lie rank.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the partition of the Hamiltonian is not expressive enough, increasing the number of layers will not reduce the error in the energy estimate, and that one should increase the reachability of the ansatz instead.
quotes: Finally, we note that if the partition of the Hamiltonian is not expressive enough increasing the number of layers will not help in reducing the error in the energy estimation.
assertions.reader_inference: The LAP result, a single optimized layer far from the ground state, is the only support in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that adding symmetry-breaking drive terms that do not commute with the problem Hamiltonian can give better ground state energies as the Lie rank increases drastically, and conclude that a higher dynamical Lie rank gives higher chances of reaching the correct ground state.
quotes: We point out that using such an approach can lead to better ground state energies as the Lie rank increases drastically.
the higher the rank, the higher the chances of the ansatz reaching the correct ground state.

assertions.value: The authors report that the rapidity of the increase of the dynamical Lie rank in the first few iterations is a viable lower bound proxy for the full calculation, balancing accuracy and computational expense.
quotes: The rapidity of the increase of the dynamical Lie rank in the ﬁrst few iterations of the calculation is found to be a viable (lower bound) proxy for the full calculation, balancing accuracy and computational expense.
assertions.reader_inference: The body supports this only through the heuristic function L(x), which needs the maximum Lie rank in advance.

assertions.value: The authors state that much remains to be done before the approach can be used readily, such as establishing systematic connections between Lie rank and methods for partitioning the problem Hamiltonian, and list extending the framework to non-problem-inspired P-PQCs and using the Lie algebra criteria to choose drive terms as future work.
quotes: A lot needs to be done before this can be used readily, such as establishing systematic connections between Lie rank and methods for partitioning the problem Hamiltonian to make an informed decision when choosing an ansatz.
Some other areas include extending the framework to non-problem-inspired P-PQCs and using the Lie algebra criteria to choose drive terms
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states these open problems in the Conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors state, as their opinion, that computing the dynamical Lie algebra is a very powerful tool for the design of ansätze because it predicts which coverage of the Hilbert space the variational optimization will explore.
quotes: In our opinion, this is a very powerful tool for the design of ansätze as one can predict which coverage of the Hilbert space will be explored through the variational optimization.
